q: Why is a free abdomen (Jackson table or Montreal mattress) important during prone spinal surgery?
o: To improve surgical access to the skin
To reduce IVC compression and epidural venous bleeding
To prevent pressure sores on the face
To allow abdominal surgery at the same time
why: A compressed abdomen raises IVC and epidural venous pressure, increasing bleeding; freeing it also improves ventilation.

q: How should the arms be positioned when prone?
o: Abducted more than 90° at the shoulder
Abducted less than 90° and directed forward, with elbows padded
why: Keep shoulders below 90° and forward to protect the brachial plexus; pad elbows (ulnar nerve).

q: Which complication of long prone spinal surgery is linked to prolonged hypotension and anaemia?
why: Avoid prolonged hypotension, particularly in long cases, to reduce the risk of visual loss.

q: After lumbar decompression, a patient develops new bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention in recovery. What is the priority?
o: Reassure: it is the spinal anaesthetic wearing off
Urgent surgical review and MRI for epidural haematoma
why: New or worsening weakness or cauda equina symptoms suggest epidural haematoma, a surgical emergency.

q: Which approach to lumbar fusion carries a risk of major vessel injury and often involves a vascular surgeon?
why: ALIF is done supine through the abdomen, close to the great vessels.

q: Which spinal metastases are very vascular and may need pre-operative embolisation?
why: Renal and thyroid metastases are very vascular; consider embolisation before surgery.

q: Which antibiotic is typically given at induction for spinal surgery (subject to local policy)?
why: Follow local guidelines: cefuroxime 1.5 g IV at induction, checking allergies.

q: What is magnesium’s role in analgesia for spinal surgery?
o: It is a potent analgesic alone
An opioid-sparing adjunct (NMDA antagonism), not an analgesic in itself
why: Magnesium is an opioid-sparing adjunct; ketamine or clonidine help in opioid-tolerant patients.

q: During spinal surgery with MEP monitoring, signals fall globally across all limbs at the same time. What is the most likely cause?
o: An anaesthetic or physiological cause (e.g. hypotension, volatile, hypothermia)
why: Anaesthetic and physiological causes tend to be global; surgical causes tend to be focal. A fall of more than about 50% in amplitude is significant.

q: Which drug increases evoked potential signals?
why: Ketamine and raised temperature increase signals; volatiles, N2O, opioids, dexmedetomidine, hypothermia and hypocapnia reduce them.
